analysis.one_liner: Lets homeowners facing foreclosure pause the process for up to 270 days while making reduced payments.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in January 2009, drew no cosponsors, and never received a committee vote before the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: During the peak of the foreclosure crisis, this bill would have given homeowners who were behind on their mortgages or facing a rate reset a court-enforceable right to postpone foreclosure for up to 270 days. During that pause, they would keep making a reduced monthly payment calculated from the loan's original terms or a standard market rate, and lenders could not charge late fees or other charges. It also would have required lenders to warn borrowers 120 days before an interest rate or payment reset, listing their options and approved counselors, and it authorized $200 million for foreclosure counseling, including legal help for homeowners.
analysis.who_benefits: Owner-occupant homeowners who were at risk of losing their homes — those who lived in the home, earned less than 200% of their area's median income, and either fell 60 days behind, faced a rate reset, or faced a payment increase. For them, the bill created a right, enforceable in court, to stop any foreclosure — including a scheduled sale — for up to nine months while they tried to catch up, refinance, or negotiate a modification. Foreclosure counseling agencies would also have gained $200 million in funding, including money to hire lawyers for homeowners.

how_it_helps.text: Gives an eligible homeowner a court-defendable right to defer any foreclosure, including a foreclosure sale, for up to 270 days while staying in the home [S3].

Caps the homeowner's required payment during the pause at the lower of the original minimum payment, a standard 30-year payment at a market rate plus a small premium, or the loan's first minimum payment, with the unpaid difference spread over the life of the loan [S3].
Bars lenders and servicers from imposing late fees or any other charges during the deferment period [S3].

Requires lenders to send a separate written notice 120 days before a rate reset or payment increase, including a good-faith estimate of the new payment and a list of alternatives such as refinancing, forbearance, and federal or state assistance [S3].

Authorizes $200 million for the Neighborhood Reinvestment Corporation for foreclosure mitigation, including counselors, translators, computers, and lawyers or legal aid agencies to represent homeowners in foreclosure [S2] [S3].
Declares a foreclosure invalid if the lender fails to notify the homeowner of the deferment right at least 30 days before starting the action and each 30 days thereafter [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders, servicers, and investors who hold the loans. They would have had to hold off on foreclosures for up to 270 days, accept reduced payments during that window, forgo late fees, absorb the paperwork of new notice requirements, and spread unpaid amounts over the life of the loans rather than recovering the property quickly.

drawbacks.text: Lenders and loan investors would absorb real losses: the deferment payment formulas could fall below the amounts owed, unpaid differences are stretched over the loan's life, and all fees during the period are prohibited [S3]. Lenders argued (in similar debates of the era) that such rules raise the cost and restrict the supply of mortgage credit.

A homeowner could keep the pause running for most of nine months while paying as little as the loan's original minimum payment — for some risky loans that initial payment was very low — meaning debt could keep growing during the pause [S3].

The bill's eligibility tied to income and occupancy would require verification and certification by borrowers, and the new notice and payment-recalculation duties would fall on servicers already overwhelmed during the crisis, inviting disputes over whether notices were proper [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the homeowners the bill targeted — owner-occupants under 200% of area median income staring at foreclosure — the benefit was direct and large: up to nine months in their home, a payment they could more plausibly afford, and no fee pile-up, with counseling money on top. The cost fell on lenders and investors as delayed recovery, reduced cash flow, and forbidding fees, which critics of such measures argued would make mortgage credit scarcer or pricier for future borrowers. The design had real rough edges — the lowest permitted payment formulas could let delinquency stretch out while debt grew — but the core trade was straightforward: buy troubled homeowners time at lenders' expense.

outcome.mechanism: Menendez introduced it the same day he filed it, the Senate sent it to the Banking Committee, and it sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a vote until the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Menendez introduced the bill on January 14, 2009, during the height of the mortgage foreclosure crisis [S1] [S3].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S5].
No further action — no hearing, committee vote, or floor vote — ever occurred; the bill died in committee when the 111th Congress ended January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders, servicers, and loan investors came out ahead: no foreclosure deferment right, no fee prohibition, and no reset-notification duties were ever enacted, and foreclosures continued under the existing rules. Homeowners received the counseling-related help that came through other legislation instead.

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Christopher Dodd (D-CT)
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it remained with the committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other senator signed on, so the partisan shape was never tested — a single Democrat introduced it, zero members of either party cosponsored it, and the Democratic-led Banking Committee never acted [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would have barred them from foreclosing for up to 270 days on eligible owner-occupants, capped their collections during that window, and banned late fees and other charges. Their gain from the bill's failure was that foreclosure timelines and fee practices stayed unchanged [S3].

Investors who held the loans would have waited longer for recovery and received reduced payments, with unpaid amounts stretched over the loan's life. The bill's death preserved faster foreclosure recovery for loan holders [S3].

industries.industry: Housing counseling nonprofits (Neighborhood Reinvestment Corporation and HUD-approved intermediaries)
industries.note: The bill authorized $200 million for foreclosure mitigation, including counselors, translators, computers, and legal aid attorneys for homeowners. This funding never materialized through this bill [S3].
